second_order: Posting and judging April Fools bait
theme_note: Participants make Siege-specific fake announcements, proposals, and dated jokes, then test, praise, reject, or extend them. What varies is whether the bait is a leak, buff, server promise, operator idea, or word joke, and whether readers are fooled or immediately call it out.

second_order: Calling people to put Siege on the canvas
theme_note: Participants publicly summon helpers for Tachanka, Rainbow6, Doc, Blitz, Valk, or a later phase. Calls range from tentative proposals and requests for help to urgent collective commands and repeated mobilization.

second_order: Routing and teaching the pixel work
theme_note: Participants make joint work actionable by supplying coordinates, Discord channels, templates, interface instructions, redirects to an existing sticky, and explanations of the five-minute pixel system. What varies is whether they orient a newcomer, consolidate duplicate efforts, or move planning off Reddit.

second_order: Saluting and joking in the Lord’s language
theme_note: Participants turn Tachanka, {-}7, ‘Sent to the team,’ and related Siege phrases into acknowledgments, reply chains, sacred-duty jokes, and morale. These codes perform group idiom around the work without by themselves specifying a practical pixel task.

Subreddit operations shape event participation by removing rule-breaking submissions, requiring direct image links, adding event flair and filters, and later judging those adjustments against the event’s end.

Participants treat the subreddit’s temporary rainbow styling as material for collective play: welcoming or resisting it, explaining it through the date, extending its pony and flair jokes, and asking what should remain. Reactions vary from delight and role-play to confusion and complaint.

second_order: Deciding what the mark should say and look like
theme_note: Participants propose and dispute the emblem’s lettering, borders, rainbow, operator additions, dimensions, and successive phases. They share design work while varying between expansive alternatives, smaller compromises, corrections, and pauses until a plan is ready.

second_order: Turning familiar game trouble into April Fools
theme_note: Participants recast crashes, disconnects, ping, and other familiar frustrations as Ubisoft’s April Fools joke, sometimes before returning to practical diagnosis. The shared practice is using the date to joke about recurring trouble; the seriousness and technical follow-through vary.

Participants report placing pixels, following a template, making progress, completing parts, and adding or changing visible features. The common practice is doing or reporting construction; its scale ranges from one square to an expanded emblem and text.

Participants maintain, repair, and defend the emblem against stray pixels, deliberate damage, scripts, or reversion. They vary between quiet cleanup, urgent attack warnings, attributing damage, and repeated calls to hold borders.

second_order: Bargaining and fighting over neighboring space
theme_note: Participants interpret nearby projects as allies, enemies, owners, or possible collaborators and negotiate boundaries, retaliation, overlap, and shared images. Relations vary and are sometimes openly disputed, especially around Bluecorner, the Hivemind, r/udub, Rainbow Road, and OSRS.

second_order: Showing and explaining what was on r/place
theme_note: Participants point others to the emblem or an update, explain what r/place is, and interpret neighboring or altered images. These acts make the canvas legible to spectators without necessarily recruiting, building, or defending it.

second_order: Claiming and thanking the shared achievement
theme_note: Participants announce success, claim collective or individual contribution, praise the emblem, thank helpers, and take pride in the room’s work. The achievement is variously described as finished, restored, shared, or still imperfect.

second_order: Arguing whether an April Fools-framed clip shows a bug
theme_note: A clip introduced as an April Fools mishap becomes a detailed dispute over misses, spread, screenshots, and confirmed Glaz hit-registration problems. Participants share the work of adjudicating the clip but differ sharply on what the frames prove.

second_order: Responding to an abandoned April Fools drawing plan
theme_note: An artist’s account of a delayed April Fools sketch plan prompts requests, praise, character jokes, and argument over an operator’s appearance. These codes stay together because they are responses to that disclosed art project, not because every reply repeats April Fools language.

second_order: Marking the canvas finished and looking back
theme_note: After placement stops, participants say the event is over, present final versions, thank contributors, inspect rogue pixels, mourn the ending, and correct obsolete proposals. The shared practice is closing or retrospectively preserving the effort rather than continuing live placement.
